Implementing Caching Patterns with Redis

Learn practical caching patterns, TTL and eviction choices, and strategies to avoid stale data, cache stampede, and cache penetration.

In this lesson

Understand patterns like Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back; implement Cache-Aside with TTL in Python; and learn how to pick eviction policies and mitigate common issues.

Why it matters

A well-designed cache reduces latency and backend load. Choosing the right pattern and TTL prevents inconsistencies and keeps memory bounded under load.

Quick takeaway

Redis is fast, but effective caching needs explicit patterns, TTLs, and eviction policy choices to remain correct and stable under load.

screens.title: Caching fundamentals with Redis
screens.narratorSegment: Caching stores copies of frequently requested data in a fast-access location so that subsequent requests return quickly without repeatedly hitting a slower primary store. Redis is often used for this because it is an in-memory store with very low read and write latencies and flexible data structures. In practice, caching reduces latency and the load on your database. For example, a product detail endpoint that is read by many users benefits from a cache: the first fetch may hit the database, but subsequent requests can be served from Redis in microseconds rather than milliseconds. When designing a cache you must decide what to cache, how long to keep it, and how to handle updates. Time-To-Live prevents data from living forever and helps limit memory usage, but TTLs introduce a window where cached data may become stale. Another design decision is whether reads should consult the cache first or whether writes should be routed through the cache. Each choice influences correctness and performance. A common misconception is that caches always speed things up without cost. In reality, caches can complicate correctness when data changes. The key takeaway is that Redis excels at accelerating reads, but it requires explicit policies for TTL, eviction, and invalidation to be reliable in production. How would you balance TTL length to favor freshness versus cache hit rate in your application?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Caching fundamentals with Redis
What is caching?

Caching is storing copies of frequently accessed data in a fast store so requests can avoid slow operations. Redis stores keys and values in memory for rapid retrieval and supports TTL to expire keys automatically.

Why Redis?
Low latency, simple key-value API, and flexible eviction policies make Redis a practical cache for many apps.
Misconception
Caches always improve performance. In reality, they add complexity: stale data, invalidation needs, and memory management must be handled.
Key Takeaway

Use Redis to accelerate reads, but design TTL and eviction rules intentionally to keep caches reliable.

Concrete example
Imagine a product page that thousands of users view per minute. Reading product details from the database for every request stresses the backend. Caching product data with a reasonable TTL returns most requests from Redis and reserves database queries for cache misses or writes.
Supporting bullets
  • Cache hit: returned from Redis, minimal latency.
  • Cache miss: application fetches from DB, stores in Redis with TTL.
  • TTL prevents permanent staleness but creates an expiry window.
  • Eviction policies decide which keys to drop when memory is full.

screens.title: Cache-Aside pattern — lazy loading
screens.narratorSegment: Cache-Aside, also known as lazy loading, is a read-first pattern where the application checks the cache before consulting the primary data store. The flow has four main steps: first, the application looks up the key in Redis; second, if the key exists, return the cached value — a cache hit. Third, if the key is missing, fetch from the primary database — a cache miss — and fourth, populate Redis with the fetched value and a Time-To-Live so future requests hit the cache. This approach caches only requested items, saving memory for rarely accessed data. A concrete example: a user profile endpoint checks cache:user:user-id, returns the profile if present, otherwise fetches from the database, stores it with SETEX and returns the fresh profile. The common drawback is initial latency for cold items and the risk of a cache stampede when many clients concurrently request the same uncached entry. You can mitigate this with a simple lock allowing one request to rebuild the cache while others wait, or by probabilistic early expiration. A misconception is that caching the whole dataset is always better; Cache-Aside intentionally avoids that by caching on demand. Think about the read pattern of your endpoint to decide whether Cache-Aside is the right starting point.

keyIdea.title: Flow summary
keyIdea.text: Check cache first, on miss fetch from DB, set cache with TTL, return data — simple and memory efficient but vulnerable to stampedes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Cache-Aside pattern
Process steps
1. Try cache GET
If value exists, deserialize and return immediately.
2. Cache miss
If missing, fetch the data from the primary database or service.
3. Populate cache with TTL
Store the result in Redis with SETEX or SET + EXPIRE so it will expire automatically.
4. Return fresh data
Return the fetched data to the client; future requests will hit the cache.
Common pitfall

Many concurrent requests for an uncached item can overload the database. Consider a lock or single-writer rebuild strategy to avoid this.

Concrete scenario

A profile endpoint first attempts GET cache:user:123. On a miss it calls fetch_user_from_db, sets the result with SETEX cache:user:123 TTL 60, then returns the profile. If many requests arrive simultaneously after expiry, use SETNX to let one request rebuild the cache while others wait or return a fallback.

Supporting tips
  • Cache only what you need to save memory.
  • Pick TTLs that trade freshness vs hit rate.
  • Consider early-rebuild or mutex to avoid thundering herds.
Check your understanding

When would Cache-Aside be a better fit than preloading all data into the cache?

screens.title: Implementing Cache-Aside in Python
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete Python example that implements the Cache-Aside pattern. The core function tries to GET a cache key. If it finds a value, it deserializes and returns it immediately. On a miss, the function fetches from the primary data source, serializes the response, and writes it into Redis with a Time-To-Live using SETEX. In practice you will import the Redis client, create a connection, and use JSON serialization for complex objects. The example in this chapter simulates a slow database call with a sleep and demonstrates cache hits after the first fetch. Important details to notice: choose a clear cache key namespace like cache:product:prod-id to avoid collisions, use decode_responses for readable strings, and handle missing database results by optionally caching a negative result with a short TTL. A misconception to avoid is embedding long-running blocking logic inside the cache write path; try to keep cache-population short and predictable. Now read the code carefully to see the GET, the conditional miss path, the SETEX call, and the manual cache invalidation via delete. Try running the example and observe the printed messages that show cache miss and subsequent cache hit behavior. After this walkthrough, you will be able to modify the TTL and verify expiry behavior in your own environment.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Cache-Aside in Python
Starter code (read-only)
import redis
import json
import time

r = redis.Redis(host='localhost', port=6379, db=0, decode_responses=True)

# Simulate a slow database call
def fetch_product_from_db(product_id):
  print(f"--- DB: Fetching product {product_id} from primary database...")
  time.sleep(1.5)  # Simulate latency
  # Return a simulated product or None
  return PRODUCT_DB.get(product_id)


def get_product_details(product_id, cache_ttl=30):
  cache_key = f"cache:product:{product_id}"

  # 1. Try to get product details from Redis cache
  cached_data = r.get(cache_key)
  if cached_data:
    print(f"--- CACHE: Hit for {product_id}!")
    return json.loads(cached_data)

  # 2. Cache miss: Fetch from the simulated database
  print(f"--- CACHE: Miss for {product_id}. Fetching from DB...")
  product_data = fetch_product_from_db(product_id)

  if product_data:
    # 3. If found in DB, store in Redis cache with TTL
    r.setex(cache_key, cache_ttl, json.dumps(product_data))
    print(f"--- CACHE: Stored {product_id} in cache with TTL {cache_ttl}s.")

  return product_data
This code shows GET, conditional DB fetch, and SETEX. Run the function twice to see a miss then a hit. To test expiry, wait for the TTL or delete the key and call again.
Example output and notes
  • First call prints DB fetch and "Stored" message; subsequent call prints "CACHE: Hit".
  • Use clear keys like cache:product:prod-001 to avoid collisions.
  • Consider caching negative results with a short TTL to prevent repeated DB hits for non-existent items.
  • Avoid very long TTLs for rapidly changing data; prefer explicit invalidation on updates.
Pro tip

When updating a product, delete the cache key right after the database write to prevent serving stale information.

screens.title: Write-Through vs Write-Back
screens.narratorSegment: Write-Through and Write-Back are two opposite approaches to handling writes when a cache is present. In Write-Through the application or cache layer writes data to both the cache and the primary database before confirming the operation. This ensures that reads from the cache see data consistent with the database, which simplifies read logic because you can always trust the cache. The downside is higher write latency since each write waits for persistence. Write-Back acknowledges the write immediately in the cache and persists the changes to the primary database asynchronously. This reduces write latency for the application, but introduces the risk of losing data if the cache fails before persistence. It also complicates consistency guarantees and error handling. A concrete scenario: use Write-Through when you require read-after-write consistency for all clients, such as a user profile update that must be immediately visible. Consider Write-Back only when you can tolerate eventual persistence and can absorb complexity for crash recovery. Don’t assume Write-Back is always faster without cost: it trades latency for risk. For most beginner deployments the Cache-Aside pattern is simpler and safer until you have infrastructure to support asynchronous durability and recovery for Write-Back.

keyIdea.text: Write-Through favors consistency at the cost of write latency; Write-Back favors low write latency but increases complexity and risk.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Write-Through vs Write-Back
Write-Through

Writes go to cache and the primary database synchronously. Reads are simple because the cache reflects the database after the write completes.

  • Pros: strong read consistency, simpler read logic.
  • Cons: higher write latency, cache stores all writes even if seldom read.
When to use

When read-after-write consistency matters and you can accept slower writes.

Write-Back (Write-Behind)

The cache acknowledges the write immediately and persists asynchronously to the database later. This reduces application-visible latency but requires mechanisms to guarantee persistence and recovery.

  • Pros: low write latency for the application.
  • Cons: risk of data loss if the cache fails before flush, more complex error handling.
When to use

Only when you have robust persistence guarantees and can tolerate eventual consistency.

Keep in mind

For beginners, Cache-Aside is the safest starting point. Choose Write-Through only when database consistency must immediately follow cache writes. Reserve Write-Back for systems with careful durability design.

screens.title: Time-To-Live (TTL) and Expiry
screens.narratorSegment: Time-To-Live is a simple but powerful mechanism to prevent cached data from living forever. In Redis you set TTLs with commands like SETEX, EXPIRE, or PEXPIRE so that keys are automatically removed after a duration. TTLs reduce stale data by bounding how long a cached value can be served, and they help control memory usage by ensuring keys eventually expire. A concrete example: store a product detail with SETEX cache:product:prod-001 30 serialized-data so it expires after thirty seconds. When choosing a TTL, think about how dynamic the data is and the acceptable staleness for your application. Short TTLs favor freshness but increase cache misses and backend load; long TTLs favor hit rate but risk serving outdated information. One mitigation is to use event-driven invalidation in addition to TTL: delete a cache key whenever the underlying record changes. Another is probabilistic early expiration to smooth expiries across clients and reduce stampede risk. A common mistake is never expiring keys and relying purely on eviction policy: this can keep stale or rarely used items in memory. TTLs are a straightforward control that, when combined with eviction policies, give you predictable cache behavior.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Time-To-Live (TTL) and Expiry
What TTL does

TTL causes Redis to automatically delete keys after a set time, preventing permanent stale entries and bounding memory usage.

r.setex("cache:product:prod-001", 30, json.dumps(product_data))  # expires after 30 seconds
Design trade-offs
  • Short TTL: fresher data, more misses.
  • Long TTL: higher hit rate, risk of stale responses.
  • Combine TTL with invalidation for critical updates.
Practical tips
  • Namespace keys clearly to make invalidation easy.
  • Use short negative-cache TTLs for non-existent keys to prevent penetration.
  • Consider slight TTL jitter or probabilistic early expiry to smooth cache rebuilds.
Key Takeaway

TTL is a simple lever to balance freshness and hit rate; choose values based on data change frequency and acceptable staleness.

screens.title: Redis Eviction Policies
screens.narratorSegment: When Redis reaches its configured memory limit, it uses an eviction policy to remove keys and free space. The policy you pick affects which data is kept and which is discarded. Common policies include noeviction, where writes fail when memory is full; allkeys-lru, which evicts the least recently used keys among all keys; volatile-lru, which considers only keys with TTL; allkeys-lfu and volatile-lfu, which evict by least frequently used metric; and random or TTL-biased policies like volatile-ttl. For caching scenarios, allkeys-lru or volatile-lru are often appropriate because they prioritize retaining recently accessed items. If you only want keys with TTL to be eligible for removal, a volatile policy will respect that. A concrete example: with maxmemory set to one gigabyte and allkeys-lru, Redis will evict the least recently used keys across the dataset to make room for new writes. A misconception is that eviction alone ensures ideal cache contents — eviction interacts with your TTLs and access patterns, so test with realistic workloads. Choosing an eviction strategy should be informed by access frequency, whether you set TTLs, and whether some keys are more critical to retain under memory pressure.

keyIdea.title: Eviction summary
keyIdea.text: Eviction policies determine which keys are removed under memory pressure; pick LRU or LFU variants based on access patterns and TTL usage.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Redis Eviction Policies
Common policies
  • noeviction: writes fail when full.
  • allkeys-lru: evict least recently used across all keys.
  • volatile-lru: evict LRU among keys with TTL.
  • allkeys-lfu: evict least frequently used across all keys.
  • volatile-ttl: evict keys with smallest remaining TTL.
Choosing a policy

Match the policy to your workload: use allkeys-lru for general-purpose caches with mixed keys, volatile-lru if only TTL keys should be removed, or LFU when hot items are identified by frequency over time.

Example scenario
For an e-commerce catalog where some product pages are highly popular, allkeys-lru preserves recently viewed products under memory pressure, keeping user experience smooth.
Performance note

Eviction decisions have runtime cost. Test your choice under realistic load to ensure eviction behavior matches expectations.

screens.title: Cache stampede (Thundering Herd)
screens.narratorSegment: A cache stampede occurs when a popular cached item expires and many clients simultaneously request it, causing a large number of cache misses that overload the backend. The root cause is synchronized expiry and high concurrency for a hot key. There are several practical defenses. One simple approach is to use a lock: when the first request detects a miss, it acquires a lock via SETNX and rebuilds the cache; other requests either wait briefly, return a degraded response, or use the stale value until the rebuild completes. Another approach is probabilistic early expiration: each read treats the TTL as slightly shorter than the configured value based on a randomized function so expiries are spread out over time. You can also use request coalescing at the application level so only one backend call occurs per missing key. A misconception is that increasing TTL always fixes stampedes; longer TTLs reduce frequency of expiry but do not prevent synchronized events if scheduled maintenance or updates invalidate keys. Choose a mitigation that fits latency and correctness needs: locks and SETNX work well for cache-aside rebuilds, while early expiry smooths load without extra coordination. Consider how you will handle waiting requests—block, retry, or serve stale—based on user expectations.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Cache stampede
Why it happens

When a hot key expires, many clients request the same resource at once. Each request sees a miss and hits the backend, causing a spike in load.

Defenses
  • Lock-based rebuild: SETNX allows a single request to repopulate cache.
  • Probabilistic early expiration: randomly refresh before TTL to stagger rebuilds.
  • Serve stale while rebuilding: return slightly stale data to avoid blocking.
Concrete pattern: SETNX lock

On a cache miss attempt SETNX lock:key with a short TTL. If SETNX succeeds, rebuild the cache and delete the lock. If not, wait or return a fallback value until the rebuild completes.

Operational note

Locks must have a TTL to avoid permanent deadlocks. Test under concurrency to verify latency behavior and safety.

screens.title: Cache penetration and negative caching
screens.narratorSegment: Cache penetration happens when requests repeatedly ask for keys that do not exist in the primary database. Each request misses the cache and hits the database, which is wasteful and can be exploited by attackers probing for many non-existent keys. A useful mitigation is negative caching: store a short-lived marker in the cache when a lookup returns no result. For example, cache a JSON null or a sentinel value for a few seconds so repeated lookups for the same non-existent ID hit the cache and avoid the database. Another defensive strategy is to use a Bloom filter to probabilistically check if an item might exist before attempting a database lookup; false positives are possible but reduce unnecessary database traffic. A common misconception is to cache negative results forever — do not do that because real data can be added later and a permanent negative cache would hide it. Choose a short TTL for negative entries and monitor for possible false positives if using probabilistic filters. Combining negative caching with rate limits and input validation further reduces the risk of penetration attacks. The practical result is fewer wasted database queries and a more resilient cache under adversarial traffic.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Cache penetration & negative caching
What is penetration?

Requests for non-existent IDs repeatedly miss the cache and hit the database. This wastes resources and can be abused in attacks.

Negative caching
Store a short-lived marker for missing keys, for example store "null" with SETEX for five seconds, so repeated requests hit the cache instead of the database.
Bloom filter option

A Bloom filter can quickly indicate if an item might exist. If the filter says 'no', you avoid a database query. Bloom filters can have false positives but never false negatives.

Caution

Do not permanently cache negative results; use short TTLs so newly created records become visible soon after insertion.

screens.title: Invalidation and stale data
screens.narratorSegment: Stale data occurs when cache contents diverge from the primary database. The simplest way to prevent stale responses after an update is explicit invalidation: delete the corresponding cache key immediately after updating the database. For critical data that must never be stale, consider Write-Through or synchronous cache updates that ensure the cache reflects the database before confirming the write. Another technique is to use short TTLs so old values expire quickly, combined with event-driven invalidation where the database publishes change events and the cache subscribes to delete or refresh keys. A misconception is that TTL alone solves stale data: TTL bounds how long data may be stale, but it does not provide immediate consistency. For distributed systems, coordinate updates through transactions or single-writer channels where possible. When invalidating, use precise keys and consistent naming so you can delete only the affected entries. Also be careful to invalidate derived caches or secondary indexes that depend on the changed data. For many applications, a pragmatic hybrid—short TTLs plus explicit invalidation on writes—balances low-latency reads and acceptable freshness. Invalidation and stale data means invalidate the exact cache key after a database update or use short ttls plus event-driven deletion to avoid stale data.. In practical terms, when and how to remove or refresh cached entries. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Invalidation and stale data
Immediate invalidation

After writing to the database, call DEL on the cache key to force subsequent reads to reload fresh data. This is the most direct way to prevent staleness.

Event-driven invalidation
Emit an event when data changes and have a cache worker listen and delete or refresh affected keys across instances.
Hybrid strategy

Use short TTLs for general freshness and explicit invalidation for critical updates. This reduces reliance on manual deletion and gives predictable expiry.

Key Takeaway

Invalidate immediately after updates for strong freshness, or use short TTLs plus events for pragmatic consistency guarantees.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why Redis is a powerful choice for a caching layer and how to apply practical caching patterns to improve performance. We will focus on the core patterns you will use in real systems — Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back — and show concrete code and strategies to handle Time-To-Live, eviction, and common problems like stale data, stampedes, and penetration. Redis gives you fast, in-memory reads and flexible data structures, but using it well requires thinking about expiration, consistency, and memory policies. For example, a simple Cache-Aside implementation can make repeated reads far faster while only caching requested items, but it also introduces the risk that many concurrent requests will hit the database when an item expires. Throughout this chapter you will see clear examples, a hands-on product catalog exercise in Python, and mitigation patterns such as negative caching and lock-based rebuilds. By the end you will understand when to pick a pattern, how TTL and eviction shape behavior, and practical steps to keep caches correct and performant. Consider how a small cache miss policy or TTL choice might change response time in your own applications.

These objectives are designed to move you from concept to practice. First, you will understand the core benefits and trade-offs of using Redis as a caching layer, including why in-memory access matters for latency and backend load. Second, you will be able to distinguish three primary caching strategies — Cache-Aside, Write-Through, and Write-Back — and explain when each pattern makes sense for read-heavy or write-heavy workloads. Third, you will implement the Cache-Aside pattern in a small application, using keys with Time-To-Live to avoid stale data while keeping memory bounded. Finally, you will reason about eviction policies and common problems such as stale data, cache stampede, and cache penetration and apply mitigation techniques like negative caching and locking. Each objective ties to a concrete skill: reading and writing cache keys with TTL, invalidating cache on updates, selecting an eviction policy, and preventing surges of backend requests. These skills let you deploy Redis safely as a cache and maintain predictable performance under load.

This second objectives screen clarifies how you will practice and be assessed. You should be able to implement the Cache-Aside pattern end-to-end: attempt a fetch, detect a miss, read from the primary store, write the result back into Redis with a TTL, and return the fresh data. You will also test behavior when a cache key expires, and when a record is updated you will demonstrate cache invalidation by deleting the corresponding cache key. For evaluation, you should explain the trade-offs between Write-Through and Write-Back: use Write-Through when strong read consistency is required and accept higher write latency; consider Write-Back only when you can tolerate complexity and potential data loss on cache failure. Finally, you will identify which eviction policies match your workload: LRU for most read-heavy caches, LFU when access frequency matters, and volatile variants when you want only TTL-bearing keys to be evicted. These skills map directly to the assessment questions in this chapter and to the hands-on product catalog activity where you will run tests showing cache hits, misses, invalidation, and TTL expiry.

Caching stores copies of frequently requested data in a fast-access location so that subsequent requests return quickly without repeatedly hitting a slower primary store. Redis is often used for this because it is an in-memory store with very low read and write latencies and flexible data structures. In practice, caching reduces latency and the load on your database. For example, a product detail endpoint that is read by many users benefits from a cache: the first fetch may hit the database, but subsequent requests can be served from Redis in microseconds rather than milliseconds. When designing a cache you must decide what to cache, how long to keep it, and how to handle updates. Time-To-Live prevents data from living forever and helps limit memory usage, but TTLs introduce a window where cached data may become stale. Another design decision is whether reads should consult the cache first or whether writes should be routed through the cache. Each choice influences correctness and performance. A common misconception is that caches always speed things up without cost. In reality, caches can complicate correctness when data changes. The key takeaway is that Redis excels at accelerating reads, but it requires explicit policies for TTL, eviction, and invalidation to be reliable in production. How would you balance TTL length to favor freshness versus cache hit rate in your application?

Cache-Aside, also known as lazy loading, is a read-first pattern where the application checks the cache before consulting the primary data store. The flow has four main steps: first, the application looks up the key in Redis; second, if the key exists, return the cached value — a cache hit. Third, if the key is missing, fetch from the primary database — a cache miss — and fourth, populate Redis with the fetched value and a Time-To-Live so future requests hit the cache. This approach caches only requested items, saving memory for rarely accessed data. A concrete example: a user profile endpoint checks cache:user:user-id, returns the profile if present, otherwise fetches from the database, stores it with SETEX and returns the fresh profile. The common drawback is initial latency for cold items and the risk of a cache stampede when many clients concurrently request the same uncached entry. You can mitigate this with a simple lock allowing one request to rebuild the cache while others wait, or by probabilistic early expiration. A misconception is that caching the whole dataset is always better; Cache-Aside intentionally avoids that by caching on demand. Think about the read pattern of your endpoint to decide whether Cache-Aside is the right starting point.

Let's walk through a concrete Python example that implements the Cache-Aside pattern. The core function tries to GET a cache key. If it finds a value, it deserializes and returns it immediately. On a miss, the function fetches from the primary data source, serializes the response, and writes it into Redis with a Time-To-Live using SETEX. In practice you will import the Redis client, create a connection, and use JSON serialization for complex objects. The example in this chapter simulates a slow database call with a sleep and demonstrates cache hits after the first fetch. Important details to notice: choose a clear cache key namespace like cache:product:prod-id to avoid collisions, use decode_responses for readable strings, and handle missing database results by optionally caching a negative result with a short TTL. A misconception to avoid is embedding long-running blocking logic inside the cache write path; try to keep cache-population short and predictable. Now read the code carefully to see the GET, the conditional miss path, the SETEX call, and the manual cache invalidation via delete. Try running the example and observe the printed messages that show cache miss and subsequent cache hit behavior. After this walkthrough, you will be able to modify the TTL and verify expiry behavior in your own environment.

Write-Through and Write-Back are two opposite approaches to handling writes when a cache is present. In Write-Through the application or cache layer writes data to both the cache and the primary database before confirming the operation. This ensures that reads from the cache see data consistent with the database, which simplifies read logic because you can always trust the cache. The downside is higher write latency since each write waits for persistence. Write-Back acknowledges the write immediately in the cache and persists the changes to the primary database asynchronously. This reduces write latency for the application, but introduces the risk of losing data if the cache fails before persistence. It also complicates consistency guarantees and error handling. A concrete scenario: use Write-Through when you require read-after-write consistency for all clients, such as a user profile update that must be immediately visible. Consider Write-Back only when you can tolerate eventual persistence and can absorb complexity for crash recovery. Don’t assume Write-Back is always faster without cost: it trades latency for risk. For most beginner deployments the Cache-Aside pattern is simpler and safer until you have infrastructure to support asynchronous durability and recovery for Write-Back.

Time-To-Live is a simple but powerful mechanism to prevent cached data from living forever. In Redis you set TTLs with commands like SETEX, EXPIRE, or PEXPIRE so that keys are automatically removed after a duration. TTLs reduce stale data by bounding how long a cached value can be served, and they help control memory usage by ensuring keys eventually expire. A concrete example: store a product detail with SETEX cache:product:prod-001 30 serialized-data so it expires after thirty seconds. When choosing a TTL, think about how dynamic the data is and the acceptable staleness for your application. Short TTLs favor freshness but increase cache misses and backend load; long TTLs favor hit rate but risk serving outdated information. One mitigation is to use event-driven invalidation in addition to TTL: delete a cache key whenever the underlying record changes. Another is probabilistic early expiration to smooth expiries across clients and reduce stampede risk. A common mistake is never expiring keys and relying purely on eviction policy: this can keep stale or rarely used items in memory. TTLs are a straightforward control that, when combined with eviction policies, give you predictable cache behavior.

When Redis reaches its configured memory limit, it uses an eviction policy to remove keys and free space. The policy you pick affects which data is kept and which is discarded. Common policies include noeviction, where writes fail when memory is full; allkeys-lru, which evicts the least recently used keys among all keys; volatile-lru, which considers only keys with TTL; allkeys-lfu and volatile-lfu, which evict by least frequently used metric; and random or TTL-biased policies like volatile-ttl. For caching scenarios, allkeys-lru or volatile-lru are often appropriate because they prioritize retaining recently accessed items. If you only want keys with TTL to be eligible for removal, a volatile policy will respect that. A concrete example: with maxmemory set to one gigabyte and allkeys-lru, Redis will evict the least recently used keys across the dataset to make room for new writes. A misconception is that eviction alone ensures ideal cache contents — eviction interacts with your TTLs and access patterns, so test with realistic workloads. Choosing an eviction strategy should be informed by access frequency, whether you set TTLs, and whether some keys are more critical to retain under memory pressure.

A cache stampede occurs when a popular cached item expires and many clients simultaneously request it, causing a large number of cache misses that overload the backend. The root cause is synchronized expiry and high concurrency for a hot key. There are several practical defenses. One simple approach is to use a lock: when the first request detects a miss, it acquires a lock via SETNX and rebuilds the cache; other requests either wait briefly, return a degraded response, or use the stale value until the rebuild completes. Another approach is probabilistic early expiration: each read treats the TTL as slightly shorter than the configured value based on a randomized function so expiries are spread out over time. You can also use request coalescing at the application level so only one backend call occurs per missing key. A misconception is that increasing TTL always fixes stampedes; longer TTLs reduce frequency of expiry but do not prevent synchronized events if scheduled maintenance or updates invalidate keys. Choose a mitigation that fits latency and correctness needs: locks and SETNX work well for cache-aside rebuilds, while early expiry smooths load without extra coordination. Consider how you will handle waiting requests—block, retry, or serve stale—based on user expectations.

Cache penetration happens when requests repeatedly ask for keys that do not exist in the primary database. Each request misses the cache and hits the database, which is wasteful and can be exploited by attackers probing for many non-existent keys. A useful mitigation is negative caching: store a short-lived marker in the cache when a lookup returns no result. For example, cache a JSON null or a sentinel value for a few seconds so repeated lookups for the same non-existent ID hit the cache and avoid the database. Another defensive strategy is to use a Bloom filter to probabilistically check if an item might exist before attempting a database lookup; false positives are possible but reduce unnecessary database traffic. A common misconception is to cache negative results forever — do not do that because real data can be added later and a permanent negative cache would hide it. Choose a short TTL for negative entries and monitor for possible false positives if using probabilistic filters. Combining negative caching with rate limits and input validation further reduces the risk of penetration attacks. The practical result is fewer wasted database queries and a more resilient cache under adversarial traffic.

Stale data occurs when cache contents diverge from the primary database. The simplest way to prevent stale responses after an update is explicit invalidation: delete the corresponding cache key immediately after updating the database. For critical data that must never be stale, consider Write-Through or synchronous cache updates that ensure the cache reflects the database before confirming the write. Another technique is to use short TTLs so old values expire quickly, combined with event-driven invalidation where the database publishes change events and the cache subscribes to delete or refresh keys. A misconception is that TTL alone solves stale data: TTL bounds how long data may be stale, but it does not provide immediate consistency. For distributed systems, coordinate updates through transactions or single-writer channels where possible. When invalidating, use precise keys and consistent naming so you can delete only the affected entries. Also be careful to invalidate derived caches or secondary indexes that depend on the changed data. For many applications, a pragmatic hybrid—short TTLs plus explicit invalidation on writes—balances low-latency reads and acceptable freshness. These cards summarize essential terms to remember. Caching stores copies of hot data in a fast-access layer to reduce latency and backend load. Cache-Aside is a lazy loading pattern where the application checks the cache first and populates it on a miss; it is simple and memory-efficient but can suffer initial latency and stampedes. Write-Through writes to both cache and database synchronously, favoring consistency but increasing write latency.
